content: There is an increased risk of developing choriocarcinoma, although this risk is lower compared to cases involving a complete hydatidiform mole. A salvage treatment regimen is initiated under the following circumstances: 1. A plateau in beta-hCG levels for three consecutive weeks, defined as a decrease of 10% or less over this period. 2. A rise in beta-hCG levels of more than 20% over two consecutive weeks. 3. The appearance of metastases. In women with complete hydatidiform moles (HM), the risk of persistent disease or neoplastic transformation approximately doubles in the presence of certain risk factors, including: Age over 35 years or under 20 years. Pre-evacuation serum beta-hCG levels exceeding 100,000 IU/L. A uterus that is larger than expected for gestational age. A large uterine molar mass. Ovarian cysts larger than 6 cm. Pre-eclampsia. Hyperthyroidism. Severe nausea and vomiting during pregnancy (hyperemesis gravidarum). Trophoblastic embolization. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). During the follow-up period, effective contraception is crucial to avoid confusion caused by rising beta-hCG levels due to a new pregnancy. Chemotherapy is required in the following scenarios: 1. A rising beta-hCG titer over two weeks (three measurements). 2. A tissue diagnosis confirming choriocarcinoma. 3. A plateau in beta-hCG levels for three weeks. 4. Persistent detectable beta-hCG levels six months after mole evacuation. 5. Evidence of metastatic disease. 6. An elevation in beta-hCG levels after previously normal values. 7. Post-evacuation hemorrhage not attributable to retained tissues. If gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) is diagnosed, the standard workup includes: Serum beta-hCG measurement. Blood tests to assess liver, renal, and bone marrow function. Chest X-ray. Pelvic ultrasound. Head CT or MRI in cases of suspected choriocarcinoma or central nervous system involvement. The treatment of GTD is determined by the risk category, as classified by the Modified WHO Prognostic Scoring System, adapted by the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO). Rare forms of GTD, such as placental-site trophoblastic tumors (PSTT) and epithelioid trophoblastic tumors (ETT), are biologically distinct and require separate management strategies. Gestational trophoblastic disease can be classified into the following categories: 1. Hydatidiform mole (HM): Complete mole. Partial mole. 2. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia: Invasive mole. Choriocarcinoma. Placental-site trophoblastic tumor (PSTT) – very rare. Epithelioid trophoblastic tumor (ETT) – extremely rare. Choriocarcinoma, PSTT, and ETT are often grouped under the term gestational trophoblastic tumors. Clinical Features of Invasive Mole and GTD The prognosis for curing GTD is generally favorable, even in cases with distant metastases, particularly when only the lungs are involved. Consequently, the traditional TNM staging system has limited prognostic value. The likelihood of cure depends on several factors: Histologic type (e.g., invasive mole or choriocarcinoma). Extent of disease spread and size of the largest tumor. Serum beta-hCG levels. Duration of disease from the initial pregnancy event to the start of treatment. Number and specific sites of metastases. Nature of the antecedent pregnancy. Extent of prior treatment. GTDs are of placental origin and contain paternal chromosomes. The most common presenting symptoms include vaginal bleeding and a rapidly enlarging uterus. GTD should be considered in any premenopausal woman presenting with these findings. Since most types of GTD are associated with elevated human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels, initial diagnostic steps include measuring hCG levels and performing a pelvic ultrasound. Additional presenting symptoms or signs may include: Pelvic pain or a sensation of pressure. Anemia. Severe nausea and vomiting (hyperemesis gravidarum). Hyperthyroidism, due to the structural similarity between hCG and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which gives hCG weak TSH-like activity. Early-onset preeclampsia during pregnancy. The most common antecedent pregnancy in GTD is a hydatidiform mole. Choriocarcinoma most frequently follows a molar pregnancy but can also occur after a normal pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, or abortion. It should always be considered in patients with persistent vaginal bleeding in the postpartum period. Other possible signs include neurological symptoms (from brain metastases) in women of reproductive age and asymptomatic lesions detected on routine chest X-rays.
